answer: Yes. The writer incorporates several sensory details that make the scene feel tangible and real. The passage appeals to the sense of touch/temperature by mentioning the "great heat of the day" ("die große Hitze des Tages") and the tightness of Herr Sander's coat made of Dutch cloth ("knapp anschließende Rock von niederländischem Tuche"). Most prominently, it appeals to the sense of sight through vivid visual descriptions of the characters' postures, gestures, and appearances—such as von Bülow's outstretched feet, his hand in his pocket, his wild gesticulations with his right hand, and Sander's black full beard, corpulent figure, and "finest white linen." Furthermore, the description of Bülow constantly speaking as if delivering a lecture appeals to the sense of sound, helping the reader to easily imagine the atmosphere of the salon.
